explanations.explanation: That's it, a tomb. God asks Shebna who authorized him “…to carve out a tomb for yourself here…” (Isaiah 22:16). He's up on the height with a chisel, picking out his own resting place in the rock. That's a lot of rock for one man to plan around.

No throne here, friend. The text says Shebna is cutting out a tomb for himself, and God asks who authorized it. A throne does show up later in the passage, but it's a different picture, and it's about Eliakim. Shebna's chisel is busy with his own resting place.

No guards and no tower in this verse. God says Shebna is chiseling a tomb for himself in the rock. The guards can relax, because nobody is building them anything. The only one getting a spot cut out of that rock is Shebna.

A wide land is right. God says He'll sling Shebna into it, and then adds, “There you will die…” (Isaiah 22:18). Notice the tomb Shebna was carving on the height isn't mentioned as the place. The text just says a wide land, and I'm not going to guess past that.

Not quite. The text doesn't say Shebna dies in the City of David. God says He'll sling Shebna into a wide land, and that's where he dies. That's a long way from home, and the verse doesn't say more than that.

Close to where he worked, but not where the verse lands. Shebna was the steward in charge of the palace, so the guess makes sense. But God says He'll roll him up and sling him into a wide land, and “There you will die…” (Isaiah 22:18). The palace isn't where it happens.

True. God says Shebna will die in a wide land, and “…there your glorious chariots will remain—a disgrace to the house of your master.” (Isaiah 22:18). Glorious chariots, and they end up a disgrace. That's quite a drop.

This one is actually true. God says Shebna's glorious chariots will remain in the wide land, “…a disgrace to the house of your master.” (Isaiah 22:18). The chariots look impressive, but the text says they end up a disgrace. Easy to doubt it, since the word glorious sounds so shiny.

Removed is right. God says, “I will remove you from office, and you will be ousted from your position.” (Isaiah 22:19). He says it twice, in two different ways, so there's no mistaking it. Shebna's time as steward is done.
No lifetime contract here. God says, “I will remove you from office…” (Isaiah 22:19). Shebna won't be finishing out his years in that job. Somebody else is already about to be called.

explanations.answer: He'll pass it to his son
explanations.explanation: No handing it down to a son. God says He'll remove Shebna and oust him from his position. Then He says He'll summon His servant, Eliakim son of Hilkiah (Isaiah 22:20). The job goes to Eliakim, and the text says nothing about Shebna's family.

Robe and sash, you got it. God says, “I will clothe him with your robe and tie your sash around him.” (Isaiah 22:21). He also puts Shebna's authority in Eliakim's hand. It's a hand-me-down, but a pretty important one.

Good guess, but those aren't the pieces named. The text says God will clothe Eliakim with Shebna's robe and tie Shebna's sash around him. No ring and no chain are mentioned in this verse. Stick with what's written, and it's a robe and a sash.

Sounds like a good traveling outfit, but that's not the list. God says He'll clothe Eliakim with Shebna's robe and tie Shebna's sash around him (Isaiah 22:21). Nothing about sandals or a staff. Eliakim is dressed from the shoulders and waist, not the feet.

Judah is right. God says Eliakim “…will be a father to the dwellers of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah.” (Isaiah 22:21). That's a big family to look after. Think of the biggest cookie order you've ever heard of, then add a whole city.
Levi isn't the name in this verse. God says Eliakim will be a father to the dwellers of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah (Isaiah 22:21). The blank is Judah, so Levi has to sit this one out.

Not Ephraim this time. The verse says Eliakim will be a father to the dwellers of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah (Isaiah 22:21). Judah is the word that fits the blank. Ephraim just isn't in the text here.

That's the opposite of what God says. The text says, “What he opens no one can shut, and what he shuts no one can open.” (Isaiah 22:22). So once Eliakim shuts something, nobody else opens it. No second set of keys is going to help.

False is right. God says, “What he opens no one can shut, and what he shuts no one can open.” (Isaiah 22:22). It works both ways, and nobody can undo what Eliakim does with that key. He's carrying it on his shoulder, so he's not going to misplace it like I used to misplace the spatula.

Firm is right. God says, “I will drive him like a peg into a firm place…” (Isaiah 22:23). A peg only works if it goes into something solid. And that firm place is where Eliakim becomes “a throne of glory for the house of his father.”

A peg in soft ground would wobble like a cookie fresh out of the oven. But the text says God will drive him like a peg into a firm place (Isaiah 22:23). Firm is the word in the verse, so firm fills the blank.

Hidden isn't in the verse. God says He'll drive Eliakim like a peg into a firm place (Isaiah 22:23). The text is about how solid the spot is, and it doesn't say anything about whether it's hidden or not.

Right. The text says they'll hang on him “…all the glory of his father's house: the descendants and the offshoots…” (Isaiah 22:24). It also lists the lesser vessels, from bowls to every kind of jar. That's a whole household hanging from one peg.

explanations.answer: The shields of the palace guards
explanations.explanation: Shields would be a nice thing to hang, but they aren't in the list. The text says they'll hang on him all the glory of his father's house, including the descendants and the offshoots (Isaiah 22:24). The palace guards aren't mentioned in this verse.

explanations.answer: The banners of the tribes of Israel
explanations.explanation: Banners would make a fine display, but they aren't in the verse. What hangs on him is the glory of his father's house: the descendants, the offshoots, and the lesser vessels (Isaiah 22:24). It stays with his family and household, with no tribes in the picture.

explanations.answer: It will give way and fall
explanations.explanation: Yes, and it's a surprise after all that firm talk. The LORD of Hosts declares, “…the peg driven into a firm place will give way; it will be sheared off and fall…” (Isaiah 22:25). The text doesn't say more about why, so I'll leave it right there. And it ends with “Indeed, the LORD has spoken.”

You'd think so, after hearing it was driven into a firm place. But the LORD of Hosts says that peg “…will give way; it will be sheared off and fall…” (Isaiah 22:25). Forever isn't in the text this time. Firm or not, the verse says it comes down.

explanations.answer: It will be moved to the temple
explanations.explanation: No moving day here. The text says the peg driven into a firm place will give way, be sheared off and fall (Isaiah 22:25). There's no temple in the verse. The peg doesn't get a new spot, it comes down.
